transcript:
>> This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Linda Kenyon.
Now that the midterm elections are over, the current Congress will return to Washington for a lame duck session.
NPR's Eric McDaniel says members who are on their way out will still have a lot to do before their time in office is done.
>> Imagine you've been told you've been laid off, but you still have to come in and work your hardest
for the next couple weeks.
Republicans have, in theory, a one- or two-vote majority in the House of Representatives,
but something tells me they could have attendance problems,
and that's going to make passing legislation even more difficult than it has been for the last two years.
They have a lot they have to get done, including the National Defense Authorization Act to fund the military and a government funding bill.
>> McDaniel says the Senate is likely to spend a lot of floor time trying to get as many judges confirmed as possible.
The new Congress will begin its term in January, with the Democrats in control in both the House and the Senate.
The Trump administration has indicated it will intervene in a Texas lawsuit against Planned Parenthood.
NPR's Shonda-Lise Duster has that story.
>> In what is regarded as an attempt to shut down Planned Parenthood,
attorneys for the Justice Department filed a notice of appearance to the United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas.
The notice follows days after Republicans, including Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, lost their seats to Democrats.
Paxton has been handling the years-long legal battle against Planned Parenthood.
The lawsuit accuses Planned Parenthood of Medicaid fraud, and the state is seeking to recover $1.8 billion.
Susan Baker Manning, general counsel for Planned Parenthood, said in a statement that the organization is going to,
"Fight this every step of the way, including at trial." NPR has reached out to the Justice Department for comment on the lawsuit,
but has not received a response.
Shonda-Lise Duster, NPR News.
>> Israel's president says he has tapped Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, to form the next Israeli government.
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot won a clear majority in last month's election, as NPR's Lauren Freya reports from Tel Aviv.
Prime Minister Netanyahu's party won slightly more seats than Gadi Eisenkot's.
But leaders of most of Israel's other parties have recommended Eisenkot be tasked with forming a government rather than Netanyahu,
who is Israel's longest-serving prime minister.
A statement from Israeli President Isaac Herzog's office says he'll hold a ceremony with Eisenkot on Sunday evening local time.
Eisenkot is a former military chief whose son was an Israeli soldier killed in combat in Gaza.
He'll have about six weeks to try to form a coalition government, after which, if he's unsuccessful, Herzog would ask someone else.
And if that person can't form a coalition, Israel could face fresh elections.
Lauren Freya, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
>> Israel held its elections on October 27th.
You're listening to NPR News.
This year's El Nino could be the strongest on record.
The natural climate pattern affects weather across the globe.
Areas across the U.S. have already felt the impact, and it is driving an El Nino economy.
NPR's Ava Berger reports.
>> Drainage contractors are very popular in California right now.
Jim Garner, who owns a construction company, says he's booked four months in advance.
>> In fact, it's to the point where I can barely keep up with it.
>> California has already seen some of El Nino's impacts, higher sea level, greater chance for coastal flooding.
But it's not just California that will see different weather this year.
Across the country, warmer and wetter conditions are forecasted for most of the continental U.S.
So a range of companies are either preparing to or are already seeing a bump in business.
We're talking tire sellers, ski mountains, and mold-sniffing dogs.
That's not a group that typically has something in common.
Thanks to El Nino, now they do.
Ava Berger and Pierre Neuse.
>> Scientists have discovered a baby right whale off the coast of Quebec.
The North Atlantic right whale is one of the rarest sea mammals in the world.
Scientists with the New England Aquarium in Boston examined photos of the calf
that said that it was likely born months ago but that it was not seen during earlier surveys that were conducted the previous winter.
The discovery brings the number of baby right whales from the recent birthing season to 24.
I'm Lyndi Kenyon, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: Congress returns to Washington for lame duck session after midterm elections
Justice Department files notice to join Texas lawsuit against Planned Parenthood over Medicaid fraud
Israeli President Herzog taps Gadi Eisenkot to form next government after inconclusive election
El Nino expected to be strongest on record, boosting business for drainage contractors and ski mountains
New England Aquarium scientists discover baby North Atlantic right whale off Quebec coast
